subtopics.name: Aging process and older adult health

questions.stem: A client with confirmed COVID-19 on droplet and contact precautions needs a nebulizer treatment and may need suctioning. Which protective equipment should the nurse wear in the room during these procedures?

options.text: A surgical mask, gown and gloves, the same as for routine droplet precautions
A fit-tested N95 respirator, eye protection, gown and gloves
Gloves alone, since the nurse will not be closer than 2 m (6 ft) for long
A cloth face covering and gloves, as long as the room door stays open

rationale.correct: Aerosol-generating procedures such as nebulizers, suctioning and intubation need an N95 respirator and eye protection with gown and gloves.

perOption.a: Aerosol-generating procedures can spread small particles; a surgical mask is not enough.
perOption.b: Aerosol-generating procedures need a respirator and eye protection in addition to gown and gloves.
perOption.c: Gloves alone do not protect from respiratory particles.
perOption.d: Cloth coverings are not PPE, and the door should stay closed.

references: CDC infection control and isolation precautions guidance

questions.stem: An unvaccinated 3-year-old arrives at a busy emergency department waiting room with a high fever, cough, red eyes and a red rash that started on the face and is spreading down the body. What should the triage nurse do first?

options.text: Have the child and parent sit in the corner of the waiting room away from other children
Put a surgical mask on the child and move them to an airborne infection isolation room
Ask the parent to take the child home and call their pediatrician in the morning
Give the child acetaminophen for the fever and register them in the usual order

rationale.correct: Suspected measles: mask the client and place them in an airborne infection isolation room right away; staff need proof of immunity.

perOption.a: Measles spreads through the air across a room; distance in a shared space does not protect others.
perOption.b: These findings suggest measles; masking the child and moving them to a negative-pressure room limits airborne spread.
perOption.c: The child needs assessment, and sending them away does not address possible exposures.
perOption.d: Treating fever before isolating allows the virus to spread in the waiting room.

references: CDC infection control and isolation precautions guidance
Pediatric nursing texts (e.g. Hockenberry, Wong's Essentials of Pediatric Nursing)

questions.stem: A unit wants to reduce falls among its older adult clients. Which intervention has the strongest evidence for preventing falls in the hospital?

options.text: Placing older clients who are confused in a vest restraint each night
Hourly rounding that checks toileting, pain and position
Keeping the room lights off at night so that clients sleep longer
Moving clients at risk to quiet rooms farther from the busy nurses' station

rationale.correct: Hourly rounding (toileting, pain, position, possessions within reach), low beds, alarms and night lights reduce falls; restraints do not.

perOption.a: Restraints increase injury and do not prevent falls.
perOption.b: Purposeful rounding meets needs that lead clients to get up alone, which reduces falls.
perOption.c: Darkness increases falls when clients get up.
perOption.d: Rooms farther away mean less observation of clients at risk.

references: Fundamentals of nursing texts (e.g. Potter & Perry)

questions.stem: The nurse's hands are visibly soiled after helping a client with incontinence. Place the steps of handwashing with soap and water in order.

items.text: Dry the hands with a paper towel and use it to turn off the faucet
Apply soap and rub all surfaces of the hands and fingers for at least 20 seconds
Rinse the hands with the fingertips pointing down
Wet the hands with warm running water

rationale.correct: Handwashing: wet, soap and rub for at least 20 seconds, rinse with fingertips down, dry and turn off the tap with the towel.

perOption.a: Water first lets the soap lather.
perOption.b: Friction on all surfaces removes dirt and organisms.
perOption.c: Water runs from cleaner to less clean areas.
perOption.d: Using the towel avoids recontaminating clean hands.

references: CDC infection control and isolation precautions guidance

questions.stem: A client is admitted for oral radioactive iodine (I-131) therapy for thyroid cancer. Which plan protects staff and visitors?

options.text: Place the client in a shared room near the nurses' station for closer observation
Use a private room, limit bedside time and flush the toilet twice
Allow pregnant visitors and children to stay as long as they wear gloves
Send the client's used linens and dishes to the regular hospital laundry and kitchen

rationale.correct: After I-131: private room, limited time and distance, no pregnant visitors or children, double flushing and radiation-safe handling of linens and waste.

perOption.a: The client gives off radiation and must be in a private room.
perOption.b: Time, distance and shielding limit exposure; I-131 is excreted in urine and other body fluids.
perOption.c: Pregnant visitors and children should not visit; gloves do not block radiation.
perOption.d: Items may be contaminated with radioactive body fluids and are handled per radiation safety policy.

references: Medical-surgical nursing texts (e.g. Lewis; Ignatavicius)

questions.educationalObjective: Plan radiation safety for radioactive iodine therapy.

questions.stem: During an infusion, an IV pump alarms repeatedly for "occlusion" even though the line is not kinked and the IV site looks normal. Another pump is available. What should the nurse do?

options.text: Keep using the same pump and silence the occlusion alarm each time it sounds
Replace the pump, tag the faulty one and report it to biomedical engineering
Run the infusion by gravity without telling anyone that the pump has stopped working
Try to open the pump and fix the sensor using a screwdriver from maintenance

rationale.correct: Malfunctioning equipment is removed from use, tagged and reported to biomedical engineering; if a client is harmed, an incident report is also filed.

perOption.a: Silencing a malfunctioning pump puts the client at risk.
perOption.b: Faulty equipment is taken out of use, labeled and reported so it can be inspected and repaired.
perOption.c: Unreported faults can harm the next client who uses the pump.
perOption.d: Nurses do not repair medical devices.

references: Fundamentals of nursing texts (e.g. Potter & Perry)

questions.stem: Which measures should the nurse expect in the plan to reduce the risk of surgical site infection for a client having elective colon surgery? Select all that apply.

options.text: Clipping hair at the site only if needed, instead of shaving
A chlorhexidine bath or wipes before surgery as prescribed
Giving the prophylactic antibiotic within 60 minutes before the incision
Keeping the client cold during surgery to slow bacterial growth
Keeping blood glucose in the target range around surgery
Shaving the abdomen with a razor the night before surgery

rationale.correct: Surgical site infection prevention: clipping not shaving, antiseptic bathing, timely antibiotics, normal temperature and glucose control.

perOption.a: Shaving causes small cuts that raise infection risk.
perOption.b: Skin antisepsis lowers bacterial counts.
perOption.c: Timing makes sure tissue levels are high during surgery.
perOption.d: Hypothermia increases infection risk; normal temperature is maintained.
perOption.e: High glucose impairs healing and immunity.
perOption.f: Razor shaving the night before increases infection risk.

references: CDC infection control and isolation precautions guidance
Medical-surgical nursing texts (e.g. Lewis; Ignatavicius)

questions.stem: A home health nurse visits a 78-year-old client with Parkinson's disease who lives alone. Highlight the findings in the nurse's note that are safety hazards.

segments.text: keeps the space heater near the bedroom curtains
Smoke detectors were tested last month
Extension cords run across the hallway to the kitchen
The bathroom has grab bars by the toilet and tub
The water heater is set to 60 °C (140 °F)
Pill bottles are lined up in a weekly organizer

rationale.correct: Home safety hazards include space heaters near fabric, cords across walkways and water heaters set above 49 °C (120 °F).

perOption.s2: Space heaters near fabric are a fire hazard.
perOption.s6: Cords across walkways are a trip hazard, especially with a shuffling gait.
perOption.s10: Water this hot can scald; 49 °C (120 °F) or lower is recommended.
perOption.s12: An organizer helps safe medication use.

references: Fundamentals of nursing texts (e.g. Potter & Perry)
Written to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 20 November 2026.

questions.stem: The parent of a 20-month-old asks when to start toilet training. Which sign best shows the child is ready?

options.text: The child turned 18 months old, which is the age when most parents start training
The child stays dry for 2 hours and tells the parent when the diaper is wet
An older sibling in the family was fully toilet trained at 20 months
The child often says "no" and wants to do things on their own

rationale.correct: Toilet training readiness: staying dry for about 2 hours, awareness of a wet diaper, walking, pulling pants up and down and following simple directions.

perOption.a: Age alone does not show readiness; most children are ready between 18 and 30 months.
perOption.b: Bladder control for a couple of hours and awareness of wetness show physical and cognitive readiness.
perOption.c: Each child develops at their own pace.
perOption.d: Independence is part of toddlerhood but does not show bladder readiness.

references: Pediatric nursing texts (e.g. Hockenberry, Wong's Essentials of Pediatric Nursing)
Written to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 20 November 2026.

questions.stem: A 12-year-old comes in for a well visit and has never received the human papillomavirus (HPV) vaccine. The parent asks how many doses are needed. What should the nurse explain?

options.text: Three doses are needed because the child is already older than 9 years
Two doses, 6 to 12 months apart, because the series is starting before age 15
One dose today, with a booster at age 18 before college
No doses yet, because the vaccine is given once a teen becomes sexually active

rationale.correct: HPV vaccine: routinely at 11 to 12 years; two doses if started before age 15, three doses if started at 15 or older or if immunocompromised.

perOption.a: Three doses are for people who start at age 15 or older or who are immunocompromised.
perOption.b: Starting before the 15th birthday needs only two doses for most children.
perOption.c: This is not the HPV schedule.
perOption.d: The vaccine works best before any exposure and is routinely given at 11 to 12 years.

references: CDC/ACIP immunization schedules
Written to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 20 November 2026.

questions.stem: A client tells the nurse they plan to try to become pregnant in the next few months. The client has no medical problems. Which supplement should the nurse recommend starting now?

options.text: Vitamin A, 10,000 international units a day to support the baby's growth
Folic acid, at least 400 mcg a day, starting before conception
Iron, 325 mg three times a day, to prevent anemia in pregnancy
Vitamin C, 2,000 mg a day to prevent infections during pregnancy

rationale.correct: Anyone who could become pregnant should take at least 400 mcg of folic acid daily, starting at least a month before conception.

perOption.a: High-dose vitamin A can cause birth defects.
perOption.b: Folic acid before conception and in early pregnancy lowers the risk of neural tube defects.
perOption.c: Routine high-dose iron before pregnancy is not recommended without anemia.
perOption.d: High-dose vitamin C is not recommended for this purpose.

references: Maternal-newborn nursing texts (e.g. Perry; Lowdermilk)
Written to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 20 November 2026.

questions.stem: A client in labor without an epidural becomes irritable, says "I can't do this anymore," and has nausea and shaking legs. Contractions are every 2 minutes and last 70 to 90 seconds. Which phase of labor is the client most likely in?

options.text: Latent phase of the first stage
Active phase of the first stage, before 6 cm
Transition, near the end of the first stage
Third stage, after the birth of the baby

rationale.correct: Transition (about 8 to 10 cm) brings intense contractions every 2 to 3 minutes, irritability, nausea, shaking and an urge to push.

perOption.a: Latent labor has milder, less frequent contractions, and the client is usually talkative.
perOption.b: Active labor brings stronger contractions, but these intense signs are typical just before full dilation.
perOption.c: Irritability, feeling out of control, nausea, shaking and strong, close contractions mark transition (about 8 to 10 cm).
perOption.d: The third stage is delivery of the placenta.

references: Maternal-newborn nursing texts (e.g. Perry; Lowdermilk)
Written to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 20 November 2026.

questions.educationalObjective: Recognize the transition phase of labor.

questions.stem: The nurse is assessing a newborn at 6 hours of age. For each finding, indicate whether it is expected or should be reported.

rows.text: Bluish hands and feet with pink lips and trunk
Yellow skin on the face and chest at 6 hours
Tiny white bumps on the nose and chin
Blue-gray patches over the lower back
Grunting with each breath and a respiratory rate of 78/min

rationale.correct: Expected: acrocyanosis, milia and dermal melanocytosis. Report: jaundice in the first 24 hours and signs of respiratory distress.

perOption.r1:c1: Acrocyanosis is common in the first day.
perOption.r2:c1: Jaundice in the first 24 hours is never normal.
perOption.r2:c2: Early jaundice suggests hemolysis and needs evaluation.
perOption.r3:c1: Milia are blocked oil glands that clear on their own.
perOption.r4:c1: Congenital dermal melanocytosis is common and harmless; it is documented so it is not mistaken for bruising.
perOption.r5:c1: Grunting and tachypnea are signs of respiratory distress.

references: Maternal-newborn nursing texts (e.g. Perry; Lowdermilk)
Pediatric nursing texts (e.g. Hockenberry, Wong's Essentials of Pediatric Nursing)
Written to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 20 November 2026.

questions.educationalObjective: Distinguish normal newborn findings from those to report.

questions.stem: An 80-year-old client brings all their medications to a wellness visit. Which medication should the nurse point out to the provider as potentially inappropriate for an older adult?

options.text: Atorvastatin 20 mg at bedtime for high cholesterol
Diphenhydramine 50 mg each night to help with sleep
Acetaminophen 500 mg up to three times a day for arthritis pain
Vitamin D 1,000 international units each morning for bone health

rationale.correct: The Beers criteria list drugs to avoid in older adults, such as first-generation antihistamines, long-acting benzodiazepines and some sedatives.

perOption.a: Statins are commonly used in older adults when indicated.
perOption.b: Diphenhydramine is strongly anticholinergic and causes confusion, falls and urinary retention in older adults (Beers criteria).
perOption.c: Acetaminophen at this dose is usually the preferred analgesic for older adults.
perOption.d: Vitamin D is commonly recommended for older adults.

references: Fundamentals of nursing texts (e.g. Potter & Perry)
Nursing pharmacology texts (e.g. Lehne; McCuistion) and the drug's prescribing information
Written to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 20 November 2026.

questions.stem: A 68-year-old man who smoked for 30 years and quit 5 years ago comes for a wellness visit. He has no symptoms. Which screening should the nurse expect the provider to recommend based on his history?

options.text: A one-time abdominal ultrasound to screen for an abdominal aortic aneurysm
A yearly chest x-ray to look for lung cancer
An exercise stress test each year to check for heart disease without symptoms
A carotid ultrasound to look for narrowing even though he has no symptoms

rationale.correct: Men 65 to 75 who have ever smoked: one-time abdominal ultrasound for AAA; lung cancer screening with low-dose CT is considered when criteria are met.

perOption.a: Men aged 65 to 75 who have ever smoked are advised to have a one-time ultrasound for abdominal aortic aneurysm.
perOption.b: Chest x-ray is not a recommended lung cancer screening test; low-dose CT is used when criteria are met.
perOption.c: Routine stress tests are not recommended in people without symptoms.
perOption.d: Carotid screening is not recommended for people without symptoms.

references: U.S. Preventive Services Task Force recommendations
Written to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 20 November 2026.

questions.educationalObjective: Identify recommended screening for an older man who smoked.

questions.stem: A client with type 1 diabetes has the flu with nausea and poor appetite. Which statement shows the client understands sick-day management?

options.text: "I'll skip my insulin doses until I can eat my normal meals again."
"I'll keep taking insulin, check glucose every 2 to 4 hours and test ketones."
"I'll drink plain water and nothing else so my blood sugar doesn't go up while I'm sick."
"I'll wait until my ketones are high before I call the provider."

rationale.correct: Sick-day rules: keep taking insulin, check glucose every 2 to 4 hours, test ketones, drink fluids, take carbohydrates if not eating and call for ketones or persistent vomiting.

perOption.a: Insulin is still needed during illness; stopping it can cause ketoacidosis.
perOption.b: Illness raises glucose; continuing insulin, frequent checks and ketone testing prevent DKA.
perOption.c: If the client cannot eat, carbohydrate-containing fluids help prevent hypoglycemia and keep up fluids.
perOption.d: The client should call early for moderate or large ketones, vomiting or high glucose that will not come down.

references: American Diabetes Association Standards of Care
Written to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 20 November 2026.

questions.educationalObjective: Evaluate sick-day teaching for type 1 diabetes.

questions.stem: The nurse is watching a parent breastfeed a 1-day-old newborn. Which observation shows a good latch?

options.text: The baby's lips are flanged outward and the mouth covers much of the areola
The parent feels sharp, pinching nipple pain throughout the whole feeding
The baby's cheeks dimple inward with each suck
Clicking sounds are heard each time the baby sucks at the breast

rationale.correct: A good latch: wide mouth, flanged lips, much of the areola in the mouth, rhythmic sucking and swallowing, and no lasting pain.

perOption.a: A wide mouth with flanged lips over much of the areola shows a deep, effective latch.
perOption.b: Ongoing pain suggests a shallow latch.
perOption.c: Dimpled cheeks suggest poor suction.
perOption.d: Clicking suggests the baby is losing suction.

references: Maternal-newborn nursing texts (e.g. Perry; Lowdermilk)
Written to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 20 November 2026.

questions.stem: A 26-year-old client is brought to the emergency department for the third time this month with sudden chest tightness, pounding heart, trembling, numb fingers and a fear of dying that peaked within 10 minutes. Heart rate is 118/min and respirations are 30/min. Today's ECG shows sinus tachycardia only, and the troponin is normal, as it was at the two earlier visits. Complete the diagram by placing the condition the client is most likely experiencing, 2 actions the nurse should take, and 2 parameters the nurse should monitor.

actions.text: Stay with the client and speak in short, calm sentences
Coach slow breathing, such as in through the nose for 4 seconds and out for 6
Explain the cause of panic disorder in detail during the attack
Leave the client alone in a quiet room to calm down
Have the client breathe into a paper bag for several minutes

parameters.text: The client's own rating of anxiety
Bowel sounds in each of the four quadrants

rationale.correct: Panic attacks peak within minutes and mimic cardiac events; after medical causes are ruled out, stay with the client, coach slow breathing and monitor breathing and anxiety.

perOption.c1: Recurrent sudden episodes of intense fear with chest tightness, palpitations and numbness that peak within minutes, with a normal cardiac workup, fit panic attacks.
perOption.c2: The ECG and repeated troponins are normal, and the pattern fits panic.
perOption.c3: Recurring episodes that resolve, in a young client without risk factors, point away from PE.
perOption.c4: Hyperthyroidism causes constant symptoms such as weight loss and heat intolerance, not brief episodes.
perOption.a1: A calm presence lowers fear and helps the client feel safe.
perOption.a2: Slow breathing reverses hyperventilation and eases numbness and dizziness.
perOption.a3: Clients in severe anxiety cannot take in detailed information.
perOption.a4: Being left alone can increase fear during a panic attack.
perOption.a5: Paper-bag breathing is not recommended and can lower oxygen levels.
perOption.p1: Slower, deeper breathing shows the hyperventilation is settling.
perOption.p2: Self-rated anxiety shows the response to calming measures.
perOption.p3: Not a guide to a panic attack.

references: Psychiatric-mental health nursing texts (e.g. Varcarolis; Halter)
Written to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 20 November 2026.

questions.educationalObjective: Recognize and respond to a panic attack.

questions.stem: A client whose surgery has been delayed twice shouts at the nurse, "This hospital is a joke! Nobody tells me anything!" What is the nurse's best response?

options.text: "Please lower your voice. Other clients are trying to rest right now."
"You're frustrated by the delays. Let me find out what's happening."
"The surgeons are very busy today, and delays like this happen to everyone."
"If you keep shouting, I'll have to call security to come and talk with you."

rationale.correct: With an angry client, acknowledge the feeling, stay calm, and offer specific actions that address the cause.

perOption.a: Asking the client to be quiet first does not address the frustration and may escalate it.
perOption.b: Naming the feeling and offering concrete help de-escalates anger and meets the client's need for information.
perOption.c: Explaining or defending the system dismisses the client's feelings.
perOption.d: Threats increase anger and damage trust.

references: Psychiatric-mental health nursing texts (e.g. Varcarolis; Halter)

questions.educationalObjective: Respond therapeutically to an angry client.

questions.stem: A client with severe depression had a second electroconvulsive therapy (ECT) treatment 2 hours ago. The client is oriented to person and place but cannot remember eating breakfast this morning. What should the nurse do?

options.text: Notify the provider right away, since memory loss suggests a stroke
Explain that short-term memory loss is common after ECT and reorient
Ask for the remaining ECT treatments to be canceled because of the memory loss
Test the client's memory by asking many questions each hour through the day

rationale.correct: After ECT, expect temporary confusion and short-term memory loss; reorient, reassure and monitor vital signs and safety.

perOption.a: Short-term memory loss around the time of ECT is expected and does not suggest a stroke.
perOption.b: Temporary confusion and memory gaps around ECT are expected and usually improve over weeks.
perOption.c: Expected memory effects are not a reason to stop a course of treatment.
perOption.d: Repeated testing increases frustration; orienting and reassuring are more helpful.

references: Psychiatric-mental health nursing texts (e.g. Varcarolis; Halter)
Written to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 20 November 2026.

questions.stem: A client in a manic episode keeps interrupting group therapy, talks over others and is giving away their snacks and money to other clients. What should the nurse do?

options.text: Ask the group members to ignore the client until the client calms down
Set calm limits, store the client's money safely and offer a quiet activity
Let the client continue in the group so that they can work off some of their energy
Tell the client they will lose their unit privileges for the rest of the week

rationale.correct: In mania, set calm, consistent limits, reduce stimulation, protect the client from impulsive acts and channel energy into simple activities.

perOption.a: Ignoring the client does not set limits or protect the client's belongings.
perOption.b: Consistent limits, protecting the client from poor judgment and reducing stimulation help in mania.
perOption.c: Allowing the behavior disrupts others and leaves the client open to exploitation.
perOption.d: Punitive threats are not therapeutic.

references: Psychiatric-mental health nursing texts (e.g. Varcarolis; Halter)
Written to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 20 November 2026.

questions.stem: A 9-year-old has had stomachaches every school morning for 3 weeks and has stopped wanting to go to recess. The pediatrician found no physical cause. What should the school nurse do first?

options.text: Tell the parent the child is pretending to be sick to avoid school
Talk privately with the child about school, friends and being bothered
Send the child home each morning as soon as the stomachache starts at school
Recommend a change to a high-fiber diet and more water to settle the child's stomach

rationale.correct: Recurrent stomachaches and avoiding school activities in children can signal bullying, anxiety or stress; ask privately and gently about school and peers.

perOption.a: Physical complaints can be real signs of stress and should not be dismissed.
perOption.b: Somatic complaints and avoiding recess can be signs of bullying or stress; a private conversation helps find the cause.
perOption.c: Sending the child home reinforces avoidance without finding the cause.
perOption.d: Diet does not address the pattern linked to school.

references: Pediatric nursing texts (e.g. Hockenberry, Wong's Essentials of Pediatric Nursing)
Psychiatric-mental health nursing texts (e.g. Varcarolis; Halter)

questions.stem: A client whose partner died 2 months ago describes how they have been feeling. Which reactions are part of normal grief? Select all that apply.

options.text: Feeling angry at the partner for not going to the doctor sooner
Trouble sleeping and a poor appetite
Briefly thinking they heard the partner's voice in the house
Having a plan to take an overdose to be with the partner
Feeling guilty about things they wish they had said
Being unable to get out of bed or eat for most days for 2 months

rationale.correct: Normal grief includes anger, guilt, sleep and appetite changes and brief sensory experiences; suicidal plans and severe loss of function need evaluation.

perOption.a: Anger is a common grief response.
perOption.b: Physical changes are common in the early months.
perOption.c: Brief sensory experiences of the deceased are common in normal grief.
perOption.d: A suicide plan is not normal grief and needs immediate assessment.
perOption.f: Severe, persistent loss of function suggests depression and needs evaluation.

references: Psychiatric-mental health nursing texts (e.g. Varcarolis; Halter)
Written to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 20 November 2026.

questions.educationalObjective: Distinguish normal grief from warning signs.

questions.stem: A nurse working a telephone advice line takes a call from a caller who says, "I've taken all my sleeping pills and I want to die." What should the nurse do first?

options.text: Tell the caller to go to bed and call back in the morning if still upset
Keep the caller on the line, get their location and send emergency help
Explain that suicide is not the answer and that things will get better with time
Ask the caller to describe why they took the pills before doing anything else

rationale.correct: With a caller who has taken an overdose: stay on the line, get the location and send emergency help, then keep the caller talking.

perOption.a: An overdose is a medical emergency.
perOption.b: Keeping contact and getting the caller's location lets help reach them quickly.
perOption.c: Reassurance does not deal with the emergency.
perOption.d: Exploring reasons can wait; the first priority is getting help to the caller.

references: Psychiatric-mental health nursing texts (e.g. Varcarolis; Halter)

questions.stem: A student who failed an exam tells the nurse, "The exam was unfair. Nobody could have passed it anyway." Which defense mechanism is the student using?

options.text: Rationalization
Regression
Repression
Reaction formation

rationale.correct: Rationalization offers an acceptable explanation for behavior or failure to protect self-esteem.

perOption.a: Giving a reasonable-sounding excuse to justify a failure is rationalization.
perOption.b: Regression is returning to an earlier stage of behavior.
perOption.c: Repression is unconsciously blocking painful memories.
perOption.d: Reaction formation is acting the opposite of how one feels.

references: Psychiatric-mental health nursing texts (e.g. Varcarolis; Halter)
